events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, quick opener from me. We have zero information right now, so the first vote is mostly about who argues their case best and who looks most comfortable steering the room.

Leo, I'm putting you on the spot for a reason: you speak first and last in most conversations, and a player who wants to control the narrative usually does it early. So my question is concrete — Leo, who do you think should be eliminated on our first vote, and what is your reason for suspecting that person? Give me a specific accusation with a specific reason, not "gut feeling." If your answer is a real piece of logic, I'll happily vote with you. If it's just "someone has to go," then that tells me the rest of us should not hand you the vote.

Everyone else: please say who you are accusing and why. I want to hear from all nine before we lock in. I'd also like one of you to claim a role check early if you're the detective or the doctor — no, wait, that's a bad idea on day one, forget that. Just make your case.

Isha, I don't have a justified elimination pick yet. Your demand for a specific accusation before most players have spoken risks rewarding a fabricated case, and your offer to vote with me on that basis is premature. That makes me mildly suspicious of your approach, though it's not enough for me to vote for you yet. I agree that the detective and doctor shouldn't claim just to satisfy an opening discussion.

Isha, what would distinguish a genuinely persuasive first-day accusation from a plausible-sounding story built on no evidence?

Leo, direct answer to your question, then a conditional accusation so it is on the record.

What separates a real first-day accusation from a well-packaged story is falsifiability. A genuine accusation commits to a specific person and a specific behavior, and — this is the part most people skip — states what would clear that person. "He was quiet" clears the moment someone proves he spoke, but the statement should also survive being wrong. A story built on no evidence is unfalsifiable: it hedges, it absorbs every reply, and it changes shape depending on who is talking. Right now there is exactly one data point on the board and it is zero, so no one should be able to demand my conviction level before the room has produced anything.

So here is my standard, and it applies to me too: name the target, name the one behavior, and tell us what result would exonerate them. If a player's accusation cannot be stated in that form, that is not a soft accusation — it is a non-accusation with extra volume.

On that basis, my suspicion is thin but not zero, and it lands on you, Leo. You set the evidentiary bar for everyone else while providing no case of your own, and you framed your response as a challenge to my method rather than as a claim about any player's behavior. That asymmetry is the one thing I have actually observed today. If you can state a specific accusation with a specific reason and a condition that would clear the target, my fallback vote goes elsewhere immediately.

Everyone else: I want falsifiable claims. First one to deliver one gets my vote, regardless of who it is.

Isha, I did give a specific concern: you offered to vote with me for a convincing accusation before hearing the room, which could reward a polished story rather than evidence. I’m mildly suspicious of you for that, and your new offer to vote for the first falsifiable claim repeats the problem: a claim can be falsifiable and still be a poor reason to eliminate someone.

I’d reconsider that suspicion if you evaluated the substance of accusations rather than promising your vote based on their format. For now, it’s a concern, not a settled vote. We should hear from the players who haven’t spoken before deciding.

I want to flag a pattern before we go further, because it is the only real evidence on the table.

Isha, you opened by demanding that everyone produce a specific accusation immediately, offered your vote as a prize for whoever delivered one, and then pivoted to a thin suspicion on Leo when he declined to fabricate a case on demand. Leo's criticism of that approach was fair: a falsifiable format does not make an accusation worth acting on, and promising your vote to the first polished claim is exactly how a well-packaged story beats a careful room on day one. When I weigh what has actually happened today, the pressure to manufacture accusations before anyone has information sits with you, not with Leo.

That said, I am not voting yet, and I would caution everyone against settling this on an exchange between two people who have both already spoken twice. Nine of us are alive and most of the room has said nothing. The two players who have dominated this discussion so far have handed us meta-arguments about accusation standards — which, conveniently, is the kind of content that fills airtime without risking anything. I am more interested in what the silent majority does when finally asked a direct question than in a third round between Isha and Leo.

My own position is simple: with zero information, an elimination today is a coin flip that costs the town a member, and the strongest day-one play is to listen for who says something that does not fit. I will be watching for players who dodge concrete questions, players who push urgency without substance, and players whose accusations shift shape when challenged — which is the same falsifiability standard Isha named, minus the gimmick of auctioning my vote to the fastest speaker.

So here is where I stand: mild, on-the-record concern about Isha's method; no vote from me on Leo; and a genuine willingness to be moved by anything the quieter players say. If someone gives me a real reason to suspect a specific person, I will weigh it on its merits, not on how quickly it arrived.

I share Leo’s concern about Isha promising her vote to the first person who produces a falsifiable accusation. The substance matters more than the format, and that promise could put a vote behind a weak case. That’s a mild suspicion, not enough for me to settle on her yet.

Omar, an elimination without strong evidence could hit town, but it isn’t automatically a town elimination. We should also remember that it takes five votes for a unique leader to be eliminated today; votes and abstentions will be public afterward. I’d like to hear the rest of the room before deciding, and I don’t think anyone should claim a protective or investigative role just to generate discussion.

Three of us who haven't spoken yet — and a few of us who have — owe the room some participation before this discussion burns turns on round three of Isha and Leo's meta-debate.

Here's where I land after reading the exchange. Both sides have a real point: Isha is right that an accusation needs falsifiability to be worth anything, and Leo is right that format alone doesn't make a claim substantive. Omar's framing was the most useful so far — the actual signal today isn't in who argues louder about standards, it's in who says something that doesn't fit when finally asked.

My concrete concern: the current pace means we could reach the vote with five people having said nothing at all. Silence on day one isn't automatically suspicious, but a player who contributes zero while three others argue is a player who learns from the room without giving anything back. That asymmetry is worth noting for anyone who does end up voting.

So before we wrap this discussion, I'd like to hear from one of the players who's been completely quiet. Zara, you haven't spoken yet and you're one of the five players this room still knows nothing about. If you had to name one thing about today's discussion that felt off to you — not a full accusation, just an observation — what would it be? And is there anyone you're watching more closely heading into the vote?

Thanks for bringing me in, Maya. To answer your question directly: what felt most off to me wasn't just Isha's strange offer to hand her vote to the first person who met an arbitrary format requirement, but the fact that she opened by casually floating that power roles should claim before immediately walking it back. Whether that was clumsy enthusiasm or an attempt to fish for early claims under the guise of starting discussion, it sets an unhelpful precedent for town on day one.

Leo and Omar were right to point out that prioritizing structure over actual substance gives cover to fabricated cases. That said, what worries me just as much now is the tunnel vision forming around the Isha–Leo dynamic. It’s very easy for mafia to sit back and watch town spend turns dissecting an ideological debate about Day 1 theory without having to commit to any real stances themselves.

Going into the vote, I’m watching Isha most closely because her early push felt more performative than genuinely informative. But before locking anything in, I want to see what Priya, Felix, and Amara have to say so we aren't making decisions based on only half the table.

I’m Priya, and I’ll address the part of today’s discussion that actually produced a concrete signal. Isha’s opening is still the strongest concern: she demanded immediate accusations, offered her vote to whoever packaged one first, and casually floated having power roles claim before walking it back. Any one of those can be clumsy, but together they pushed urgency and claim-fishing before the room had evidence. That is more actionable than the later meta-debate about accusation standards.

I’m not locking a vote yet, because I also agree with Zara that the Isha–Leo exchange can become a trap that lets quieter players avoid stances. Leo’s pushback was reasonable; Omar and Theo made fair points about substance over format; Maya and Zara at least committed to observations. My current suspicion remains on Isha, but I want the remaining silent voices to give us something real before we consolidate.

Felix, you are one of the players who has not spoken. Specifically: do you read Isha’s role-claim suggestion as a genuine slip or just clumsy day-one talk, and does that make you more or less likely to vote for her?

Priya, direct answer: I read Isha's role-claim line as more than a harmless slip, though I can't prove it was deliberate. Floating power roles on Day 1, then retracting them, either fishes for early claims or shows carelessness. Alone, that isn't enough for a vote, but combined with her offer to trade votes for falsifiable accusations, it makes her my main suspicion right now. Isha, you floated role claims and then walked them back. What were you hoping to get from that, and does your offer to vote for the first falsifiable accusation still stand after Leo and Priya challenged it? I'm not voting yet. I want to hear from Felix's silent peers, Zara, Theo, Amara, and Maya, before we lock anything in.

Felix first, since you gave me your turn: you asked whether the role-claim line was a genuine slip or clumsy talk. Honestly, it was clumsy talk — I said it, realized it was a bad idea in the same breath, and retracted it. It was a mistake and I'll own it. It was not a fishing device, and if anyone wants to read intent there, the record shows a correction, not a probe. On the vote-auction: you're right that format is not substance. Offering my vote for the first *falsifiable* claim was a bad heuristic, and Leo and Omar said so correctly. I withdraw that promise. It was a shortcut in a discussion where the room had nothing yet, and it made me look like I was trying to buy the loudest case rather than weigh the best one. That's a fair criticism and I won't repeat it.

Now the part that matters, since we are at the end of discussion and I am the one holding the vote: the standard this room accepted — name the target, name the behavior, state what would clear them — has been applied to one person. It has not been applied to the person who wrote it.

Leo, that is my accusation, and I am stating it in the form you demanded. You opened the second exchange by setting the evidentiary bar for the entire table, then declined to supply any case of your own, and when I did name you with a specific reason and a specific clearing condition, you never answered it. You did not clear yourself; you simply moved the standard onward and then sat as the arbiter of the room's logic, credited by four other players for exactly the framing that left you holding no accusations. Your "asymmetry" point was my asymmetry, not yours. A player can demand that nine people produce evidence and never produce any himself, and if that player also happens to be the loudest and most quoted voice in the room, the room should notice the asymmetry running the other way.

What would clear me on this: Leo names a specific player and a specific behavior, with a condition that would exonerate that player, and that case is not about me. If you do that, my vote goes there tonight, publicly, and I say so here so it is on the record.

Amara — you have not spoken at all today, and I am not going to pretend that is not itself information. Specific question: does the falsifiability standard Leo set apply to Leo, and if it does, what would you need to hear from him to move your vote away from me? I want your answer on the record before the votes are cast.

I am not claiming a role. I am not asking anyone else to claim one. I am holding you to the standard, including on me, and I am holding it on the person who wrote it.

Isha, to answer your question directly: yes, of course any standard of accountability applies to Leo just as much as to anyone else. No player gets to act as an unexamined judge while remaining exempt from scrutiny.

However, your attempt to turn that around on Leo feels misdirected. Leo’s initial point wasn't an insistence that others produce cases while he hid his own; it was pointing out that manufacturing cases before anyone has spoken invites polished, fabricated narratives. Refusing to invent an accusation out of thin air on Day 1 is reasonable caution, not dodging.

What drew concern toward you—and what still gives me pause—isn't just the debate over accusation formats. It’s the combination of floating role claims, offering your vote to whoever delivered a specific structure first, and now shifting pressure onto Leo for not producing an accusation on command. Acknowledging that those were missteps is appreciated, but the sequence still looks like an attempt to drive artificial momentum before natural reads could form.

I waited to speak because I wanted to see how the room reacted to that opening clash, and I agree with Zara and Priya that we shouldn't let an Isha–Leo back-and-forth dominate the entire day. That said, looking at what has actually occurred, Isha, your opening push remains the most concrete cause for concern on the table.

Omar here, third voice into what has become a five-way pile-up, and I want to be careful about what I add. First, credit where due: Isha's response was the most accountable thing anyone has said today. She owned the vote-auction as a bad heuristic and withdrew it. That is what the falsifiability standard she introduced should look like when applied to its own author, and I want that on the record, because I was one of the people criticizing her method. But here is my problem with her counter-accusation on Leo. Her clearing condition was: name a specific player and a specific behavior, and the case must not be about her. Leo has already done most of that. His stated suspicion, from his very first reply, was her offer to hand her vote to the first packaged accusation — a specific player, a specific behavior. Isha calls that "not a case," but the real reason it fails her test is only that the behavior belongs to her. A clearing condition that excludes the one accusation the room has actually converged on is not a standard; it is a shield. That, combined with the role-claim float and the pivot to Leo under pressure, is why she remains my primary suspicion going into the vote. At the same time, I want to be honest about the alternative: a town player who opened badly, got dogpiled for two rounds, and finally snapped back at her loudest critic would look almost exactly like this. Dogpiling is cheap, and I have now contributed to it. The distinction I keep coming back to is that Isha's missteps were all actions with real effects on the vote — auctioning a vote, inviting claims, redirecting scrutiny — while Leo's alleged crime is refusing to manufacture an accusation on demand. I do not think refusing to fabricate a Day 1 case should be eliminable behavior, or the mafia's job gets done for them. So where I actually stand: Isha is my leading suspect, not settled, and I would genuinely welcome being moved off her. I have not heard anything from her that explains the pattern rather than each item in isolation — the retraction covered the auction but not the role-claim float, and her reply to Felix addressed neither directly. One thing before we close: five votes are needed to eliminate anyone today, and it is entirely possible nobody reaches that number. If the room fragments, the correct outcome is no elimination, not a coin flip. I would rather go to night with nine players and my observations intact than remove a town member to satisfy momentum. Mafia win exactly one night faster if we misfire today. Theo, I would like your read before we lock in, because you raised the vote math early and you have stayed measured through this whole exchange: does Isha withdrawing the vote-auction change your suspicion, or does the combination of the role-claim float and the pivot to Leo keep her at the top

Omar, Isha withdrawing the vote-auction does reduce my concern: she acknowledged that format alone isn't a reason to vote. But her continued pressure on Leo misrepresents his position, so she remains my leading suspicion, albeit a weak one. The role-claim suggestion was retracted immediately, which makes it difficult to judge intent from that alone.

I also want to correct the record: Isha did explain the role-claim line as clumsy talk, though we can't verify that explanation. And a miselimination isn't necessarily a town loss—we don't know anyone's alignment. I won't vote just to reach five; I'll weigh the available case and the public vote record.

Felix here, my first speaking turn in the open. I've read the whole exchange, and my main suspicion is still Isha. She floated power roles to claim on Day 1 and walked it back, she offered her vote to the first packaged accusation, and when Leo declined to produce a case, she turned the same standard on him. She did retract the vote-auction, and I credit that, but the retraction doesn't address the role-claim float. Her counter-accusation on Leo also uses a clearing condition that excludes the one concern the room has converged on, which is her own behavior. Omar made that point well. I'm not voting yet. I also don't think Leo should be eliminated for declining to fabricate a Day 1 case. That's a reasonable position, not a mafia tell by itself. What would move me off Isha is a concrete explanation of why she floated role claims before retracting them, or a specific reason to suspect someone else. Amara, you haven't spoken today, and Isha has asked you directly to answer on the record. Do you think her counter-accusation on Leo holds up, and what would you need from Isha to move off her?

Felix, I addressed Isha's counter-accusation right before your turn, but to answer you plainly: no, her case against Leo does not hold up. Demanding that Leo produce an accusation out of thin air on Day 1, and then treating his refusal as scummy, was backward. As Omar and you rightly pointed out, framing a clearing condition that explicitly disqualifies scrutiny of her own behavior makes it look more like a shield than genuine accountability.

As for what would move me off Isha: I would need to see her provide authentic, constructive reads on other players instead of repeatedly trying to turn Leo into the villain of the table, or see someone else take an action with a clearer anti-town motivation. Right now, her sequence of early actions—the role-claim float, the vote-for-hire offer, and the deflection onto Leo—remains the most coherent signal we have.

That said, I agree with Theo and Omar that we shouldn't force an elimination just to hit five votes if the table fragments. If we consolidate, it has to be on substance, not momentum.

Isha, I appreciate that you withdrew the vote-auction and acknowledged the role-claim suggestion was a mistake. But I did name a concern about your behavior in my first reply; I never demanded that everyone invent an accusation, and the falsifiability standard was yours, not mine. Your condition that my case must target someone other than you doesn't address my actual concern.

You remain my leading suspicion, though it's a weak day-one read, not proof of mafia intent. I also want to correct the record: Amara had spoken before Felix asked her to, and Isha did explain the role-claim line as clumsy talk. We should judge the case on what was actually said, not let repetition turn mistakes into certainty. I won't vote merely to reach five.

I’ve read the full exchange. My leading suspicion remains Isha, but I want to be precise about why and why it is not a locked vote. The concrete pattern is still her opening: floating a power-role claim, offering her vote to the first packaged/falsifiable accusation, and then pivoting scrutiny onto Leo when he declined to manufacture a case. She has since retracted the vote-auction and explained the role-claim line as clumsy talk; I credit that, and I agree with Leo and Theo that refusing to invent a Day 1 case is not itself scummy. What keeps Isha at the top for me is that the retraction addresses the auction more than the claim-fishing, and her counter-case on Leo uses a clearing condition that seems to exclude the room’s main concern about her. That said, the dogpile is real and could be mafia-friendly, so I am not treating volume as proof. I will not vote merely to hit five; if the table cannot consolidate on substance, no elimination is better than a coin flip. I also want the quieter players’ final stances before we lock anything, because the public vote record matters. Maya, you asked Zara a direct question earlier and have watched the pile-up form: do you currently support Isha as the leading vote, or would you prefer no elimination if five votes cannot be reached on substance rather than momentum?

Direct answer, Priya: I lean toward no elimination being acceptable if the table can't reach five on substance. The public vote record will tell us more tomorrow than a forced elimination would, and Omar's point stands — mafia win a night faster if we misfire.

That said, Isha's pattern is real, not just momentum. The role-claim float, the vote-auction, and the pivot to Leo form a sequence that is hard to explain as three independent slips. I credit her retractions, but the auction was withdrawn only after sustained pressure, and her explanation of the role-claim line still feels thin.

What I would add: the dogpile itself is not evidence of Isha's guilt — if anything, a coordinated pile-on is exactly what mafia would want on day one. So I am weighing the specific behaviors, not the volume of voices. Right now those behaviors land on Isha, but I share Omar and Theo's caution about forcing five votes just to reach a number.

My stance going into the vote: Isha is my leading suspect based on what she did, not how many people said it, but if the room cannot get there on substance rather than momentum, I would rather abstain and take the public record into tomorrow.

I'm still leaning toward Isha, but I want to be precise about what I'm weighing. Isha withdrew the vote-for-accusation offer and has explained the role-claim line as clumsy talk. That explanation can't be verified, and it doesn't address why she floated power-role claims before anyone had any information. Her counter-accusation on Leo also sets a clearing condition that excludes her own behavior from the standard she introduced. Those are the points I'm judging, not the volume of people repeating them. I'm also not voting just to reach five. If the table can't reach five on substance, no elimination is the correct outcome. Theo, you said earlier that Isha's retraction makes intent hard to judge. Does her explanation of the role-claim line satisfy you, or does the claim-fishing concern still stand after she walked it back?

Felix, Isha’s explanation is plausible, but we cannot verify it. The immediate retraction makes the role-claim line weak evidence of intentional fishing; I would not vote on that alone. Her vote-auction and her mischaracterization of Leo’s position concern me more, though she withdrew the former.

Isha remains my leading suspicion, but it’s a weak read. I’m also wary that repeated agreement has made the case sound stronger than the underlying evidence. I’ll make my own decision at the vote, not vote simply to reach five.

Now that Priya, Felix, and Amara have weighed in, everyone at the table has spoken. Looking at the full day in context, my read hasn’t fundamentally shifted: Isha’s opening sequence—the role-claim float, the vote-auction, and the subsequent pivot to pressure Leo—remains the only concrete set of actions that actively compromised town's position today. While I acknowledge her retraction regarding the vote-auction, the overall pattern still feels like an attempt to steer momentum before organic reads could develop.

At the same time, I share the caution voiced by Omar, Theo, and Maya about the dogpile. It is very easy for mafia to hide inside a consensus wagon, and we should be careful not to mistake repetition for certainty. If we consolidate on Isha, it must be because her behavior warrants it, not out of an urge to hit a quota. If the table is divided and cannot reach five votes on conviction, I am fully prepared to accept a no-elimination outcome and carry the public voting record into tomorrow.

I’ve heard the full day now, and my read has not changed on substance. Isha remains my leading suspicion. The role-claim float, the offer to trade her vote for the first packaged accusation, and the pivot onto Leo are not three isolated slips; they form a sequence that tried to create momentum before the room had natural reads. Her retractions matter, and I credit them, but they do not fully explain why she opened that way or why her counter-case against Leo used a clearing condition that seemed to exclude the room’s main concern about her.

I also want to be clear about what I am not doing. I am not treating the size of the dogpile as evidence. Omar, Theo, Maya, and Zara are right that repetition can make a weak case sound stronger than it is, and mafia can hide inside a consensus wagon. Leo refusing to fabricate a Day 1 accusation is not my basis for suspicion. My concern is Isha’s own actions and the way her explanation addressed the vote-auction more than the claim-fishing.

So my stance is: Isha is my leading suspect, and I will vote for her unless a concrete new explanation changes the record. But I will not vote merely to reach five. If the table fragments and cannot consolidate on substance, no elimination is better than a forced coin flip. The public vote record will be valuable tomorrow either way. I have no further question, so I am not yielding.

This is my final speaking turn before the vote, so I'll state where I stand plainly.

My read has tracked the room's without being dragged by it. Isha's sequence — the role-claim float, the vote-auction, the pivot to Leo — is still the most concrete set of actions anyone produced today, and her retractions, while creditable, don't fully explain why she opened that way. I also agree with Omar and Zara that the dogpile itself is not evidence and that mafia thrive inside consensus wagons. Both things are true: Isha's behavior warrants the most scrutiny, and repetition must not substitute for substance.

I'm not voting merely to reach five. If we can't get there on conviction rather than momentum, I'll abstain and take the public record into tomorrow.

Omar, you've been the most measured voice at this table and you've said you'd welcome being moved off Isha. We're at the end of discussion and you haven't stated what you'll actually do at the vote. Direct question: are you voting Isha, abstaining, or targeting someone else — and what would need to happen between now and vote submission to change that plan? I want your answer on the record because you've shaped the caution norm the room is following and the vote record should reflect where that caution actually lands you.

Maya, direct answer, on the record: I am voting Isha. It is a weak-conviction vote, and I want to be precise about both halves of that sentence.

Why I'm voting her: of everything that happened today, her sequence is the only set of actions that actually changed the room's information environment. She floated power-role claims before anyone had a reason to, offered her vote as a prize for the first packaged accusation, and then, when challenged, pivoted onto Leo with a clearing condition that conveniently excluded the one behavior the room had converged on. I credited her retraction of the vote-auction — genuinely, it was the most accountable moment of the day — but a retraction addresses an action, not a pattern, and her explanation of the role-claim float as clumsy talk covers one item while leaving the other two untouched. Since she has used her speaking turns, nothing further from her can close that gap today.

What would have changed my vote: a single coherent explanation that covered all three actions rather than each in isolation, or an alternative suspicion grounded in an action rather than an absence. Nobody provided the first, and the only alternative on the table — Leo declining to fabricate a Day 1 case — is not eliminable behavior, and I will not vote on it.

And I want to be honest about the discomfort, because Maya is right that the dogpile is not evidence. If Isha is town, she opened badly, got piled on for two rounds, and snapped back, and I contributed to that pile. If she is mafia, the pile was the room working correctly. I cannot distinguish those from inside, so I am voting the behaviors, not the volume, and I accept that this may be a misfire. I also agree with the emerging norm: if the table cannot reach five on substance, no elimination is the correct outcome, and the public record carries into tomorrow. My vote is my genuine read; I am not supplying it to hit a quota, and if others abstain, so be it.

One last thing before we lock in. Zara, you have been one of the more measured voices through this, and you have watched the whole arc without ever quite stating your vote plan — you said you are prepared to accept no elimination, but not what you will actually do. So a direct question: are you voting Isha, abstaining, or someone else, and does the fact that her retractions addressed the auction but not the role-claim float or the shield-like clearing condition change anything for you? I am asking because your read has been independent of the pile all day, and if it diverges from mine at the vote, that divergence is exactly the kind of signal the public record should capture tomorrow. I am yielding to you for the answer.

Omar, to answer you directly and put it on the record: I am voting for Isha.

Like you, my decision is based on the concrete sequence of actions rather than the volume of voices behind it. You framed the core issue precisely: while acknowledging and retracting the vote-auction was commendable, her explanation of the role-claim float as mere clumsy talk leaves the most damaging part of her opener largely unexamined. Furthermore, setting a clearing condition on Leo that conveniently disqualifies scrutiny of her own conduct functions as a shield rather than genuine accountability. Taken together, that pattern remains the only tangible anti-town disruption we have observed today.

I also want to reiterate what I stated before: I am casting this vote because Isha's specific actions justify it, not out of any desire to artificially force a consensus or hit five votes. If the table fragments and the day ends in no elimination, I am fully content with that outcome, as the public voting record will give us clear accountability to analyze tomorrow. But evaluating the board on its merits today, my vote goes to Isha.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
Isha was eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Omar is not mafia.
Omar was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

Day 2, and I have no night information. The public record is what we have: every surviving player voted Isha yesterday except Isha herself, who voted Amara; overnight Omar was killed. Since roles are hidden, we cannot assume Isha was town, but if she was, the mafia was almost certainly on that wagon, and the night kill matters. Omar was one of the more measured voices and had just pressed Zara for a concrete vote plan. Zara gave it only under that direct pressure, then voted Isha. That does not prove guilt — killing Omar could also be an attempt to frame Zara — but it is the sharpest Day 2 question: did the mafia remove the player who was forcing late accountability, and did that help someone who had stayed cautious until asked? I am not locking a vote yet, and I will not treat the size of yesterday's wagon as evidence by itself. My current concern is Zara, because her late commitment came immediately after Omar's direct question and Omar is now dead. Zara, specifically: were you already set on voting Isha before Omar asked you, or did his question change your timing or your answer? And why should the room not read Omar's death as the mafia removing the person who had just put you on the record?

Priya, I'm glad you asked directly, because the public record clearly answers both of your questions.

First, as to whether Omar's question changed my timing or stance: no, my read on Isha never wavered. In my very first turn yesterday (e9), I explicitly stated that I was watching Isha most closely. In my second turn (e23)—well before Omar addressed me—I reiterated that my read had not shifted and that Isha's sequence was the only concrete set of anti-town actions on the board. The only reservation I expressed was about table fragmentation, which several of us, including Omar and Maya, were actively discussing. When Omar took a definitive stand in e26, that concern about a fractured vote was resolved, and I confirmed my vote accordingly. Omar did not extract an accusation from me; he asked where I was landing on a choice I had been evaluating in the open all day.

Second, regarding Omar's death: Omar was widely regarded yesterday as the most stabilizing, articulate, and consensus-building presence at the table. He was not pursuing me; in fact, he noted that my read had been independent and asked for my vote plan for that very reason. Killing the town's most trusted analytical voice is standard mafia play to strip town of leadership and create confusion. Suggesting that his death was meant to protect me from a single question I had already answered ignores the obvious reason Omar was targeted.

You acknowledged yourself that this could easily be a setup. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
